newsitem.title: USA: Stable prices in reach for major nations - Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: Stable prices in reach for major nations - Greenspan.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan Friday commended major nations and other countries around the world for making significant progress in bringing down inflation over the past 15 years.

"Now, for the first time in at least a generation, the goal of price stability is within the reach of all the major industrial countries as well as a substantial number of others," Greenspan said in prepared remarks for a meeting of central bankers and economists on monetary policy.
Greenspan said that as the economy has become more complex in the latter part of the 20th century, it has become more difficult to get a precise measurement of the actual level of price changes.
As officials from the Fed and economists gathered here for their annual meeting, a debate was brewing about how aggressive the central bank should be in combating inflation.

The debate is more than just academic, and its outcome will affect the economy and the nation's financial markets. Long-term interest rates again have jumped above 7 percent in the bond market in the past two days as investors worry that surprising strength in the economy will prompt the Fed to raise rates later this year in a bid to ward off inflation.
But whether to raise short-term rates in the current environment, when inflation has been subdued despite the economy's strength, is at the heart of the current debate.

The debate comes with inflation hovering below 3 percent for four straight years -- the lowest the economy has sustained since the 1960s. But after a surge in economic growth last spring, some Fed policy-makers fear that if the momentum continues, inflation might pick up.

The government said Thursday that the economy grew even more quickly last spring than the rapid pace first reported, raising doubts that a second-half slowdown will occur soon enough to head off higher interest rates.

But it also said there was little sign that prices were heating up. The implicit price deflator, a key measure of inflation, rose at a 1.8 percent annual rate in the quarter -- the same as estimated a month ago, and down from a 2.2 percent rate in the first quarter.
Inflation in Europe also remained steady in July, rising at an annual rate of 2.5 percent, the European Union's statistical office said Friday.

In his remarks, Greenspan said that a proposal by the U.S. Treasury to index government bonds for inflation "may not be as helpful as one might suppose" in helping to keep track of expectations regarding inflation.
"Indexed to what?" the Fed chairman asked. "Is there a specific aggregate price level index for both evaluation and possible indexing on which we can rely?"
Nevertheless, Greenspan stressed the importance for central banks of being able to judge when they are achieving their long-run goal of price stability.
